sources_considered.why: Controlled comparisons of human and neural-network image recognition.
The researchers' dated demonstration of conspicuous physical-object misclassification.
Primary evidence that some apparently strange machine judgments remain understandable to humans.

evidence_items.publisher: Geirhos et al., ICLR paper hosted on arXiv
evidence_items.locator: Section 3.1, Texture vs shape bias in humans and ImageNet-trained CNNs

receipt.public_excerpt: CNN recognition accuracies were much lower than human accuracies.

evidence_items.explanation: Humans and networks classified the same images differently. The experiments also identified differing reliance on shape and texture.

evidence_items.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Our process works for arbitrary 3D models'

receipt.public_excerpt: classifies as an espresso at every angle!

evidence_items.explanation: The authors demonstrated a physical object that produced a conspicuously unexpected classification across viewpoints. This supports the ordinary claim about surprising failures.

receipt.public_excerpt: Human intuition may be a surprisingly reliable guide to machine (mis)classification

evidence_items.explanation: Across adversarial-image experiments, people could often anticipate machine labels. This limits any stronger claim that deep-learning behavior is wholly unintelligible or never human-like.
